newsitem.title: USA: Dow Jones index closes above 6,600 for first time.
newsitem.headline: Dow Jones index closes above 6,600 for first time.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average closed above 6,600 points Tuesday for the first time, setting its second consecutive record as a wave of bargain hunting swept the market.

The Dow ended up 33.48 points at 6,600.66, surpassing Monday's record of 6,567.18. In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,483 to 1,030 on active volume of 538 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq index also set a record, rising 11.33 points to 1,327.73.
Analysts said Tuesday's session produced a somewhat broader rally than Monday, when the Dow rose 23 points, and saw the Dow index overcome an early loss of more than 50 points.
"This makes me feel a little bit better about the market," said Gregory Nie, technical analyst at Everen Securities. "The comeback this afternoon keeps the door open for the bulls to take control."
Even so, Nie said, the rally was at best a "half-step" forward for stocks. "The rally continues to focus on the upper crust and at some point that becomes troubling," he said.

Analysts said the market also benefited from the so-called "January effect," a period when stocks are boosted by a flow of cash into mutual funds from corporated bonus payments, dividend distributions and annual retirement account contributions.
"This is invariably one of the strongest periods for mutual funds," said Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities.
"There is a natural inclination to put that new money to work, which does explain why January tends to be a successful month for the market," he said.
The flow of investment money also helps explain why stocks have managed a pair of record performances despite weakness in the bond market.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond lost nearly a quarter point, which raised its yield to 6.79 percent from 6.77 percent Monday. The yield moves in the opposite direction to the price.
Analysts said one worry was sidestepped when Newt Gingrich became the first Republican in 68 years to win a second consecutive term as speaker of the House of Representatives.

"I think it eliminates a cloud over the market because another speaker might not have shown the same dedication to a balanced budget," said Phil Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.
Among individual issues, Santa Fe Pacific Gold Corp. rose 1 to 15-1/4 after receiving a sweetened takeover offer from Newmont Mining Corp., whose stock fell 3/4 to 40-1/2.
Homestake Mining Co., which has reached a friendly merger deal with Santa Fe, rose 9/16 to 13-11/16. Homestake said it still planned to complete its transaction with Santa Fe.

UST Inc. fell 2-5/8 to 30-3/4 after warning that its fourth quarter sales and earnings would fall short of analysts' estimates. The company cited lower-than-expected sales of its smokeless tobacco products. UST owns Skoal and Copenhagen, the two leading brands of smokeless tobacco.
General Instrument Corp. rose 1/2 to 23-1/4. The company announced a broad restructuring under which it will split into three publicly-traded companies.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 5.58 points to 753.23. The American Stock Exchange index rose 3.57 to 575.63.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 2.62 to 396.90. The average share was up 27 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was at a new high of 7,299.147 up 45.712 or 0.63 percent.
